docs.ab.p1: Load reference… opens your system's file dialog, or drop a file on the window. It reads WAV, AIFF, FLAC and MP3, up to 20 minutes, and the bar shows the file's name, its length and its loudness. B plays the reference from where your DAW is (from the start in the standalone app), A is your chain, and each switch is a 20-millisecond crossfade.
docs.ab.p2: Match loudness plays the reference at your vocal's loudness, so you judge the tone and not the level. The reference is kept in memory only: it is never saved with your project, a preset or anywhere else, and a file on a network drive is refused.
docs.ab.p3: Compare keeps two versions of your chain. A is the one you are editing; press B and it starts as a copy, so nothing changes; edit it, and A and B each keep their own. Both are saved with your project.
docs.ab.title: A/B
docs.agreement.p1: The first time Takelight opens it shows its licence agreement and its disclaimer. Until you agree, it does nothing but pass your audio through unchanged, so declining never silences a track.
docs.agreement.p2: Your answer is kept on your computer and shared by every open copy of Takelight, in every DAW and in the standalone app. You can read the agreement again and accept it at any time.
docs.agreement.title: The licence agreement
docs.automation.p1: Each slot owns 24 host parameters, named after the slot (F1 to B4), and a module's knobs and switches take them in order, so your DAW can automate them. The list of parameters never changes when you add, swap or remove a module.
docs.automation.p2: A few settings are not automated, because changing them mid-note would click: an EQ band's type and slope, a filter's slope, and modes such as the de-esser's detection. They are saved with your project all the same.
docs.automation.title: Automation
docs.browser.p1: Type in the search at the top — an artist, a nickname or a genre — or press Ctrl+K (Cmd+K on a Mac) from anywhere. The chains appear as you type: each artist with its eras, each era with its years and its roles, such as lead, ad-lib or FX. Choose one and the whole chain loads in order, click-free, while the track plays. The arrow keys move through the list, Enter loads, and Escape closes it.
docs.browser.p2: With the search empty, it offers the chains you loaded last. An artist with no chain yet offers chains from their genre, and a name it does not know says so and suggests a genre.
docs.browser.p3: Version 0.6.0 has Drake in three eras — So Far Gone (2009), Take Care (2011) and the modern era (2016–2026) — with an FX chain from the Take Care era; forty more artists, era by era; and a lead and an ad-lib for every one of the 73 genres, trap in two decades. The roster page lists them all. Each chain is named for its artist or genre and its era, and nothing more.
docs.browser.title: Finding a chain
docs.cards.p1: Beside its knobs, each module's card draws what it does, worked out from the same maths that makes the sound. The EQs — Parametric, Console and Program — draw their curve over your vocal as it plays: its spectrum before the EQ, dim, and after it, bright, with the peaks held for a moment. Each band has a dot on the curve: drag it to move the band's frequency and gain together, turn the mouse wheel over it for its width, double-click it to put the band back, or use the arrow keys. A whole drag is one step to undo. The De-esser draws the band it listens to and the cut it makes, and Trim its high-pass.
docs.cards.p2: The compressors, the Level Rider and the Limiter draw their curve — the level in against the level out — with a dot where your vocal sits on it now, and beneath it the gain reduction of the last four seconds. A steady note puts the dot on the curve; a sharp attack can lift it above for a moment, before the compressor catches it. Drag the threshold along the curve, or use the arrow keys: it turns the knob that sets it. The Gate's card shows the level it hears against its threshold, shaded where it is shut.
docs.cards.p3: The Delay draws its repeats on a timeline against your project's beat and bar, each as loud as the feedback and filters leave it; Ping-pong's left repeats sit above the line and its right ones below. The Reverb draws its decay — the pre-delay, the early reflections and the tail — and the Reverse Gate its swell. The Doubler, the Chorus and Width show the stereo field from above, and Saturation, the Exciter and Lo-fi show their curve and the harmonics it adds to your vocal as it is now.
docs.cards.p4: Only the cards on screen draw, and up to eight EQ cards show your vocal's spectrum at once. Tune has its pitch graph instead, and the Shifter its knobs alone.
docs.cards.title: What each card shows
docs.disclaimer.p1: Artist names identify a style, and nothing more. Freally Takelight is not affiliated with, endorsed by, sponsored by or approved by any artist, producer, engineer, label, publication or plugin maker. All names and trademarks belong to their owners, and no artist's likeness, logo, signature or artwork is used anywhere.
docs.disclaimer.p2: A chain applies processing; it does not change who is singing, and no chain promises any particular sound. Takelight's modules are its own designs and do not claim to be any other product.
docs.disclaimer.p3: This is a summary. Takelight shows the full disclaimer with its licence agreement.
docs.disclaimer.title: The disclaimer
docs.inputCheck.p1: Input Check, at the top of the rack, sets you up before you record. Press it and sing or play the take for ten seconds; the take light glows amber while it listens. It needs at least two seconds of voice, and asks again when it heard too little.
docs.inputCheck.p2: Then it shows what it heard — the peak, the level, the loudness, the noise floor, the rumble under 80 Hz, the sibilance and the plosives — and what it suggests: the Input knob, to bring your voice to a healthy level, and the gate's threshold, the high-pass and the de-esser's threshold. It sets only the modules your chain already has; one it lacks says Not in this chain, and nothing is added for you.
docs.inputCheck.p3: Nothing changes until you press Apply, and Undo takes the whole Apply back in one step. Discard leaves everything as it was. If the take clips, it asks you to lower your interface's gain, because clipping can't be undone after recording.
docs.inputCheck.title: Input Check
docs.intro: This manual grows with every version. Right now it covers finding a chain, your presets, Simple mode and its four knobs, A/B, the rack and what each card shows, undo, its four effect returns, Tune, Input Check and its thirty modules.
docs.lamp.p1: The take light at the top of the rack glows green while a module is in the rack and your voice is coming in, flashes red when the input clips, and stays dark otherwise. It turns amber while Tune's Auto Key is listening for the key, and while Input Check listens.
docs.lamp.p2: The In and Out meters on either side show the left and right channels, and beside the In meters the Input knob sets the level coming in, from −24 to +24 dB; your DAW can automate it. Each has a clip light that stays lit until you click it. A compressor's card shows how much it is turning the vocal down, while it is.
docs.lamp.title: The take light and the meters
docs.language.p1: Takelight and this site speak eighteen languages, with Arabic laid out right to left. Artist names are never translated.
docs.language.title: Languages
docs.modules.autopan.p1: Moves the vocal from side to side on a sine or a triangle wave, with rate and depth: a balance, so each side keeps its own sound and at the centre both pass as they came in; toward one side the other fades, never louder than it came in.
docs.modules.autopan.title: Auto-pan
docs.modules.chorus.p1: A two-voice chorus, one voice rising in pitch as the other falls, with rate, depth, mix and drive; at a 50 % mix it keeps the level and sums to mono cleanly.
docs.modules.chorus.title: Chorus
docs.modules.console.p1: A mixing console's channel EQ: high- and low-pass filters and four bands, in four characters — British E, British G, Class A and Proportional Q.
docs.modules.console.title: Console EQ
docs.modules.deesser.p1: Tames harsh "s" sounds, split-band or wideband, with a bell or a shelf, and relative or absolute detection.
docs.modules.deesser.title: De-esser
docs.modules.delay.p1: Five characters — Digital, Tape, Analog, Ping-pong and Slap. Its time is set in milliseconds or as a note value from 1/64 to two bars, triplets and dotted notes among them, in time with your project. Filters in the feedback, ducking under the vocal, and width; above 100 % feedback the repeats swell and hold instead of running away.
docs.modules.delay.title: Delay
docs.modules.doubler.p1: Turns one take into two, three or four voices, each a little late, drifting a little in time and pitch, and spread across the stereo field, in a Tight and a Wide character. Summed to mono, it stays close to the vocal's own level.
docs.modules.doubler.title: Doubler
docs.modules.dynamiceq.p1: Two bands, a bell or a shelf each, whose gain moves with the level in their own part of the vocal: a negative range cuts a harsh or boomy region only when it gets loud, a positive one lifts it as the voice rises. Each band has a frequency, Q, threshold, ratio and range, with one attack, release and output.
docs.modules.dynamiceq.title: Dynamic EQ
docs.modules.exciter.p1: Adds harmonics above a frequency you choose — odd, even or a blend of both — for presence and air. Only the harmonics are added; the vocal itself passes through untouched.
docs.modules.exciter.title: Exciter
docs.modules.fet.p1: Fast and forward, with fixed ratios and an All setting for aggressive compression, and a Mix control for parallel compression.
docs.modules.fet.title: FET Compressor
docs.modules.flanger.p1: A short delay swept slowly up and down and fed back into itself, with rate, depth, delay, feedback and mix; the right side sweeps a quarter of a cycle ahead of the left, so a mono vocal flanges across the stereo field.
docs.modules.flanger.title: Flanger
docs.modules.gate.p1: A gate or an expander between phrases, with hold, hysteresis and sidechain filters so breaths and bleed do not open it.
docs.modules.gate.title: Gate
docs.modules.limiter.p1: A true-peak limiter: the output never rises above its ceiling, even between samples.
docs.modules.limiter.title: Limiter
docs.modules.lofi.p1: Fewer bits and a lower sample rate, from 24 bits down to 4 and from 48 kHz down to 1 kHz, with dither, an anti-alias filter, drive and a Mix control.
docs.modules.lofi.title: Lo-fi
docs.modules.multiband.p1: Splits the vocal into low, mid and high bands at two crossovers and compresses each on its own, with a threshold, ratio and gain per band and one attack, release, knee, output and mix. With nothing taken, the bands add back up to the vocal as it was.
docs.modules.multiband.title: Multiband Compressor
docs.modules.opto.p1: Smooth levelling that follows the performance, from one Peak reduction knob, in an Opto and a Tube opto character, compressing or limiting.
docs.modules.opto.title: Opto Compressor
docs.modules.p1: Version 0.6.0 has thirty modules. Each is Takelight's own design, and none claims to be any other product.
docs.modules.parametric.p1: Eight bands, each a bell, a shelf, a cut or a notch, with cuts from 6 to 96 dB per octave. Its knobs show one band at a time — choose the band by its number — and every band has its dot on the curve.
docs.modules.parametric.title: Parametric EQ
docs.modules.phaser.p1: A chain of 4, 8 or 12 all-pass stages swept by a slow wave, fed back and blended with the vocal, with rate, depth, frequency, feedback, stages and mix; the right side sweeps a quarter of a cycle ahead of the left.
docs.modules.phaser.title: Phaser
docs.modules.program.p1: Broad, gentle boosts and cuts at the low and high ends, and a tube stage for warmth.
docs.modules.program.title: Program EQ
docs.modules.punch.p1: A character compressor in five characters, from Normal to Distortion 3, with Nuke for extreme compression and a Mix control.
docs.modules.punch.title: Punch Compressor
docs.modules.reverb.p1: Five characters — Plate, Room, Hall, Chamber and Ambience — with pre-delay, a decay from 0.1 to 20 seconds, size, damping, diffusion, modulation and filters on the return. The decay is the time the tail takes to fall by 60 dB.
docs.modules.reverb.title: Reverb
docs.modules.reversegate.p1: The reverse reverb: after each sound, a wash that swells over the gate length, from 50 ms to a second, and stops dead. It never looks ahead, so it adds no latency and works while you record.
docs.modules.reversegate.title: Reverse Gate
docs.modules.rider.p1: Rides the vocal's level toward a target loudness — up for the quiet words, down for the loud ones — within a range and at a speed you set, and leaves the breaths between phrases alone. An optional 10 ms look-ahead lets it move just before a word; it adds 10 ms of latency, which Takelight reports to your DAW.
docs.modules.rider.title: Level Rider
docs.modules.saturation.p1: Tape, Tube, Transformer, Inflate and Clip, oversampled so the harmonics it adds stay clean; Clip holds the peaks at full scale over a short, smooth knee.
docs.modules.saturation.title: Saturation
docs.modules.shifter.p1: Moves the voice up or down by up to two octaves, its formants moved on their own by up to an octave, with a Mix control: the ad-lib an octave down. Like Tune, it waits 21 milliseconds, or 4 while Tracking.
docs.modules.shifter.title: Shifter
docs.modules.title: The modules
docs.modules.trim.p1: Gain, polarity and a high-pass filter with a choice of slope: the first thing in most chains.
docs.modules.trim.title: Trim
docs.modules.tune.p1: Pitch correction to a key — Auto Key, Chromatic or one of the 24 — with Retune speed from 0 to 400 ms, Humanize and Flex, and a graph of the pitch sung and tuned. One per rack; see Tune and Auto Key above.
docs.modules.tune.title: Tune
docs.modules.varimu.p1: A tube compressor whose ratio rises the harder it works, so it starts gently and holds firm, with six time constants; 5 and 6 let go more slowly the longer it has been compressing.
docs.modules.varimu.title: Vari-mu Compressor
docs.modules.vca.p1: Clean and precise, in a Bus and a Channel character, with RMS or peak detection, a sidechain high-pass and a Mix control.
docs.modules.vca.title: VCA Compressor
docs.modules.vox.p1: Evens out a vocal's level with just a threshold and an output.
docs.modules.vox.title: Vox Leveler
docs.modules.width.p1: Narrows or widens the stereo image, from mono at 0 % to 200 %, without changing the mono sum, and a Haas delay of up to 30 ms on the right side to spread a mono vocal.
docs.modules.width.title: Width
docs.presets.p1: Save preset… at the top keeps the chain as you have shaped it — every module, knob, send and fader, and Simple's four knobs — under a name you choose. Each preset is a file in Documents › Freally Takelight › Presets, so you can back it up or send it to someone.
docs.presets.p2: My presets… lists them, each with the chain it was made from, to load, rename, export or delete. Import… brings in a preset someone sent you, numbering its name if you already have one by that name. A file that is not a Takelight preset, is larger than 256 KB or was saved by a newer version is refused, and the list says why.
docs.presets.p3: Your presets are in the search too, under My presets. When the chain a preset was made from is updated in a later version, the preset loads onto the updated chain and keeps every change you made, and says so.
docs.presets.title: Your presets
docs.privacy.p1: The plugin and the standalone app never go online: no account, no telemetry, and no networking code, which a build gate refuses. Your vocals never leave your computer, and a reference file you load for A/B is kept in memory only.
docs.privacy.p2: From version 1.0, a separate helper checks for updates and activates your licence — only when you ask. It never downloads or installs anything.
docs.privacy.title: Privacy and the network
docs.project.p1: Your project keeps the chain, every module and knob, the view, Simple's four knobs, both sides of the compare and what Tune listens to. If a project's settings cannot be read, it opens on the default chain and says so once, above the stage, until you dismiss it.
docs.project.title: Saved with your project
docs.rack.p1: The rack holds the whole chain in signal order, in four rows: the Front end (slots F1 and F2), the Inserts (I1 to I12), the four effect Returns (A to D, slots R1 to R12) and the Bus (B1 to B4).
docs.rack.p2: Choose a module from an empty slot's menu to add it. Its card shows every control it has: knobs for values, switches, and menus for options. Its header holds its character, when it has more than one, Bypass (B), Solo (S) and the × that takes it out.
docs.rack.p3: Every change is click-free. A module you add or take out fades in or out, a new character crossfades, and every knob glides, so you can work while the track plays. A bypassed module keeps its latency, so your DAW stays in time.
docs.rack.p4: Every control works from the keyboard. Tab moves between them; the arrow keys turn a knob, and Shift turns it in bigger steps; Home and End take it to either end; a double-click puts it back to its default.
docs.rack.p5: A rack holds as many knobs as Takelight can move at once — every slot full of the largest modules would be more — so past that, a module is refused and the rack says it is full.
docs.rack.title: The rack
docs.report.p1: Write to freallyproducts@gmail.com. When Takelight itself fails, the message it shows offers Report: it opens a page in your own browser showing everything it would send, and nothing leaves your computer until you press Send. After a crash, the next launch offers the same.
docs.report.title: When something goes wrong
docs.returns.p1: Each of the four returns, A to D, is fed from the end of the Inserts row by its Send knob, from off to +6 dB. The vocal goes through the return's three slots — a delay and a reverb, say — and the return's fader sets how much of it joins the dry vocal on its way into the Bus.
docs.returns.p2: Hold a return's Throw key and the vocal is thrown into it: its send rises to 0 dB, and falls back when you let go, over 5 milliseconds either way. Throw A to D are host parameters too, so your DAW can record a throw and play it back — a delay tail on one word.
docs.returns.p3: A delay set to a note value keeps time with your project's tempo, and follows it when the tempo changes during the song.
docs.returns.title: Returns and throws
docs.settings.p1: Settings chooses light or dark and the language, among other things. Your choices belong to the computer, not the project: they apply to every copy of Takelight on it.
docs.settings.title: Settings
docs.simple.p1: Simple shows the take light, the chain's name, four large knobs and the In and Out meters; Advanced, from the switch at the top, shows the whole rack. Your project remembers which view you left it in, and Settings chooses where a new one opens.
docs.simple.p2: Tune sets how fast and how naturally the vocal is tuned. Tone makes the chain darker or brighter, around 1 kHz, and the de-esser follows. Space turns every effect send up or down together, by up to 12 dB. Amount sets the whole chain against your dry vocal, from dry at 0 % to the full chain at 100 %.
docs.simple.p3: With Tune, Tone and Space at the centre and Amount at 100 %, the chain plays as it was made, and every chain loads that way. Each knob is a host parameter, so your DAW can automate it, and a double-click puts it back.
docs.simple.title: Simple mode and the four knobs
docs.start.p1: Takelight runs inside your DAW as a CLAP, VST3 or AU plugin, or on its own as a standalone app. Put it on a vocal track. It opens in Simple mode: search an artist or a genre, pick an era and a role, and the whole chain loads. Until you load a chain or add a module, your audio passes through unchanged.
docs.start.p2: There are no downloads before version 1.0.0, and the code is private.
docs.start.title: Getting started
docs.tune.p1: Tune pulls each sung note to the nearest note of its key. Retune speed sets how fast: at 0 ms the voice jumps from note to note, the hard, stepped sound; slower, it glides there, and at a few hundred milliseconds the tuning is hard to hear. Humanize lets long notes settle more slowly, and Flex keeps the scoops and vibrato that wander furthest from the note. The voice's formants stay where they are, so it keeps its character, and breaths and consonants pass through untouched.
docs.tune.p2: The Key menu starts on Auto Key: Tune listens to your vocal and settles on its key within about four seconds of singing, tuning to the nearest semitone until then, while the take light glows amber. The card says the key it hears, and Lock keeps it. Or choose Chromatic, or any of the 24 keys yourself. If no key is heard after 20 seconds of singing, the card asks you to choose one.
docs.tune.p3: The pitch graph shows the last four seconds: the pitch you sang as a thin line and the pitch Tune sends on as a green one, over a line for the note it is pulling to.
docs.tune.p4: To hear a note before it tunes it, Tune waits 21 milliseconds, and Takelight reports that to your DAW, so the vocal stays in time with the beat. While you record, that wait would be in your headphones, so the Tracking host parameter, on Auto, drops Tune to 4 milliseconds whenever your DAW records, and the card says so. Set Tracking to On or Off to choose yourself.
docs.tune.p5: A rack holds one Tune, because one Tune tunes the whole vocal.
docs.tune.p6: Auto Key can find the key from the beat instead. Send the beat to Takelight's sidechain input in your DAW and set Listens to, on Tune's card, to Sidechain: Tune follows the beat's chords. Your project remembers the choice, and Settings sets it for new ones. While nothing plays on the sidechain, Tune listens to your vocal, and the card says so.
docs.tune.title: Tune and Auto Key
docs.undo.p1: The arrows at the top undo and redo every change to the sound, up to 100 steps: a knob (a whole drag is one step), a module added or taken out, its character, Bypass and Solo, the sends and faders, Simple's four knobs, the Input knob, a chain or a preset loaded, and Input Check's Apply. Ctrl+Z undoes, and Ctrl+Shift+Z or Ctrl+Y redoes (⌘Z and ⌘⇧Z on a Mac), while Takelight's window has the focus, so your DAW keeps its own shortcuts.
docs.undo.p2: The view, the theme, the language and the A/B reference are never undone, and neither is your DAW's automation. Each project starts with a fresh history when it opens, and so does each side of the compare when you switch to it.
docs.undo.title: Undo and redo
features.title: What is in it
featuresPage.cards.chains.body: Type an artist, pick an era and a role — lead or ad-lib — and the whole chain loads in order: inserts, effect returns and the vocal bus.
featuresPage.cards.chains.title: Artist-and-era chains
featuresPage.cards.daw.body: CLAP and VST3 on Windows, macOS and Linux, AU on macOS, and a standalone app. Saved with your project, latency reported so your DAW lines everything up, and safe in many instances at once.
featuresPage.cards.daw.title: In every DAW
featuresPage.cards.inputCheck.body: Input Check listens to ten seconds of your take and sets the Input knob, and the gate, the high-pass and the de-esser your chain has. A/B compares the chain against a reference file you load, loudness-matched, or against a second version of itself; the reference is never stored.
featuresPage.cards.inputCheck.title: Input Check and A/B
featuresPage.cards.joint.body: One rack holds the whole chain: pitch correction, four kinds of EQ, six kinds of compressor, a de-esser, a gate, saturation, an exciter, lo-fi, a limiter, a doubler, a chorus, a flanger, a phaser, an auto-pan, delays, reverbs, four returns and a vocal bus.
featuresPage.cards.joint.title: The Joint
featuresPage.cards.lightDark.body: A dark mode and a light mode, both in Freally green, with every knob, fader and switch rendered in Blender for each, and the take light that glows when the chain is live.
featuresPage.cards.lightDark.title: Light and dark
featuresPage.cards.modes.body: Simple shows four macros — Tune, Tone, Space and Amount. Advanced shows every module as rendered hardware, each card drawing what it does — the EQ curve over your vocal, the compressor's curve and what it takes — and every knob can be automated.
featuresPage.cards.modes.title: Simple and Advanced
featuresPage.cards.offline.body: No account, no telemetry and no model. The plugin and the app never go online; update checks and licence activation run in a separate helper, only when you ask.
featuresPage.cards.offline.title: Offline, private, no AI
featuresPage.cards.swap.body: Change chains while the track plays. The new chain is made ready away from the audio and crossfaded in over 30 milliseconds, so nothing pops.
featuresPage.cards.swap.title: Swaps without a click
featuresPage.cards.title: What version 1.0 does
featuresPage.cards.tune.body: Pitch correction from classic signal processing, with the key found from your vocal or a sidechain, and a low-latency mode for recording through it.
featuresPage.cards.tune.title: Tune and Auto Key
featuresPage.coming.downloads: There are no downloads before version 1.0, and none on this page.
featuresPage.coming.intro: Stated plainly, because a feature list that hides its gaps is not worth reading. This page is version 1.0, and Takelight is built one rung at a time: not everything on it is built yet. Each rung on the road to 1.0 is marked with its state.
featuresPage.coming.title: What is still coming
featuresPage.compare.asOf: Takelight's column is version 1.0, which is not out yet. The other products change too; this table is as of October 2026. Product names belong to their owners and are used here only to compare.
featuresPage.compare.intro: Freally Takelight 1.0 next to the vocal plugins producers reach for when they want a named sound. Every cell for another product comes from its maker's pages or published coverage, checked in October 2026; a cell they do not settle says not verified.
featuresPage.compare.ourPrice: One price, once, after a free trial
featuresPage.compare.row.key: Finds the key from your vocal
featuresPage.compare.summary: Only Takelight has chains by artist, era and role, all three plugin formats, Linux as well as Windows and macOS, and no AI at all.
featuresPage.compare.theyWin: Muze has 52 artist presets today and runs in Pro Tools; Takelight's first artist chains arrived with version 0.5.0, and it is not a Pro Tools plugin at 1.0. CLA Vocals and The Spirit were made with the engineer and the producer they are named for.
featuresPage.compare.title: Side by side with the commercial tools
featuresPage.free.body: Nothing is for sale and nothing is downloadable before version 1.0. Then there is a free trial of the whole plugin, and one price, paid once: no subscription and no account. The audio you make with it is yours.
featuresPage.free.title: Nothing to buy yet
featuresPage.lead: One vocal plugin with a whole vocal chain for each artist and era — tuning, EQ, compression, de-essing, delays, reverbs and the vocal bus — built from its own modules.
featuresPage.limits.aax: It is not a Pro Tools plugin (AAX) at 1.0.
featuresPage.limits.match: It does not match your vocal to a reference automatically; Vocal Match is planned for after 1.0.
featuresPage.limits.roster: It does not have every artist. The roster grows with each version.
featuresPage.limits.title: What 1.0 does not do
featuresPage.limits.voice: It does not change who is singing, and it never imitates a voice.
featuresPage.numbers.borrowed: impulse responses, samples or copied presets
featuresPage.numbers.macros: macros: Tune, Tone, Space and Amount
featuresPage.numbers.plugin: plugin for the whole chain, with no other plugin to buy
featuresPage.numbers.plugins: plugin formats, plus a standalone app
featuresPage.numbers.returns: effect returns, plus a vocal bus
featuresPage.numbers.systems: operating systems: Windows, macOS and Linux
featuresPage.version: This page describes Freally Takelight version 1.0: everything on it is in 1.0, and nothing planned for after 1.0 is on it.
featuresPage.why.built.body: Every module is Takelight's own classic signal processing. No impulse responses, no samples, no borrowed code, and no settings copied from another product's presets.
featuresPage.why.built.title: Built, not borrowed
featuresPage.why.local.body: No telemetry and no cloud. Your vocals never leave your computer, and a build gate fails if networking code is ever added to the plugin or the app.
featuresPage.why.local.title: It stays on your machine
featuresPage.why.names.body: A chain is named for the artist and the era, and nothing more. No likeness, no cover art, and no promise to make anyone sound like anyone.
featuresPage.why.names.title: Honest names
featuresPage.why.reference.body: A/B sets a reference file you load beside your vocal at the same loudness, so the louder one never fools your ears. The reference stays in memory and is never saved.
featuresPage.why.reference.title: Your reference, level-matched
featuresPage.why.roster.body: Artists and genres share their names with Freally MIDI Master and Freally Unloop, so one roster runs through the whole Freally line.
featuresPage.why.roster.title: One roster for the family
featuresPage.why.title: Why it is built the way it is

hero.cycle: One plugin.|On your vocal.|In every DAW.
hero.headline: Every era’s vocal chain. One plugin.
hero.sub: Search an artist, pick an era, press play. Takelight loads the whole vocal chain — tuning, EQ, compression, de-essing, delays, reverbs and the vocal bus — built from its own modules. Offline and 100% AI-free.
honest.downloads.body: No beta on this page, no preview build, no early access. Version 1.0 comes with a free trial of the whole plugin and a one-time licence.
honest.downloads.title: There are no downloads before 1.0.0
honest.network.body: The plugin and the standalone app contain no networking code at all, and a build gate fails if any is added. Update checks and licence activation will live in a separate helper that acts only when you ask.
honest.network.title: It never goes online
honest.start.body: A chain is where your vocal starts, not a promise of a sound. Turn the macros, open the rack and make it yours; nothing you change is ever locked.
honest.start.title: A chain is a starting point
honest.title: The things most sites put at the bottom
honest.voice.body: A chain reproduces processing: tuning, EQ, compression, delays and reverbs. Your voice, your microphone, your room and your delivery stay yours, and no preset makes anyone sound like someone else.
honest.voice.title: A chain is not a voice
ladder.intro: One line per version. This is the same ladder the private plan follows — if one moves, both move, and a build gate compares them.
ladder.note: A version that is done is built and tagged. It is not a download: there are none, and there will not be until 1.0.0.
ladder.rung.v0.1.0: The foundation: the plugin loads as CLAP, VST3 and AU and as a standalone app, passes your audio through untouched, asks you to accept its licence, and every quality gate runs.
ladder.rung.v0.2.0: The Joint: one rack for a whole vocal chain, the first EQ, dynamics and colour modules on rendered hardware, and the take light.
ladder.rung.v0.3.0: Space: delays, reverbs, doubling, width and the four effect returns, in time with your project.
ladder.rung.v0.4.0: Tune: pitch correction from classic signal processing, the key found from your vocal, and a low-latency mode for recording.
ladder.rung.v0.5.0: First light: search an artist and an era, and the whole chain loads in one click. The first complete version.
ladder.rung.v0.5.5: Input Check, ad-lib chains, your own presets, and undo.
ladder.rung.v0.5.6: Visual cards: every module shows what it does — the EQ curve over a live spectrum of your vocal, the compressor curve with what it takes — not just knobs.
ladder.rung.v0.6.0: The first wave of artist chains, a chain for every genre, and the roster page.
ladder.rung.v0.7.0: In every DAW: saved with your project, automatable, its latency reported, and safe in many instances at once.
ladder.rung.v0.8.0: The standalone app at full strength, and Takelight on macOS and Linux.
ladder.rung.v0.9.0: The second wave of artist chains, and a realism and performance pass.
ladder.rung.v0.9.5: Reference Match: load a reference, and Takelight reads the delays, the reverb, the tone and the rest of its vocal, and proposes them on its own modules.
ladder.rung.v1.0.0: The release: the free trial, the one-time licence, and the first downloads this site has ever offered.
ladder.rung.v1.0.0-beta: Hardened: installers for three systems, the update check, the trial and the licence, and the full manual. Still no downloads on this site.
ladder.rung.v1.0.0-rc: The release candidate: every file reviewed and every host tested by hand.
ladder.rung.v1.1.0: Vocal Match: your vocal's tone set against a reference you own.
ladder.rung.v1.2.0: Doubles and harmonies, stacked for you.
ladder.rung.v1.3.0: A third wave of artist chains, and chains sent in by producers.
ladder.rung.v1.4.0: Bridges to Freally MIDI Master and Freally Unloop.
ladder.rung.v1.5.0: Pro Tools as a plugin (AAX), if Avid's terms allow it.
ladder.title: The road to 1.0

site.tagline: Every era’s vocal chain. One plugin.
what.p1: A raw vocal does not sound like a record, and the gap is a chain: tuning, EQs, compressors, a de-esser, delays and reverbs on sends, and a vocal bus, in the right order, at the right settings.
what.p2: Takelight holds a whole chain for each artist and era inside one plugin, built from its own modules, so you never need another plugin to hear it.
what.p3: Load a chain and it crossfades in without a click. Shape it with four macros, or open the rack and turn any knob.
what.title: What it is
